full_judgment:
20. In contracts for sale of immovable property, the fact that a specific time is fixed for payment or for conveyance does not normally make time of the essence. Failure to pay at a fixed time is not per se sufficient to terminate the seller's duty to convey; and failure to convey on the exact date does not per se discharge the buyer. In such agreements, usually time is not the essence of contract, the reason being that the law of equity which governs rights of the parties in cases of specific performance of contracts of sale of immovable property, looks not at the letter but at the substance of the agreement The intention to treat time as the essence of the contract may be evidenced by circumstances which are sufficiently strong to displace the normal presumption that in a contract for sale of real estate, stipulation as to time is not the essence of the contract. 

 23. The supreme Court, however, by majority maintained the trial Court's judgment which dismissed the suit for specific performance on the reasoning’s that the plaintiff failed to establish that he was since the date of the contract, continuously ready and willing to perform his part of the contract, which he failed to establish by adducing reliable evidence; that the trial Court rightly dismissed the suiton the said ground and that the plaintiff did not challenge the finding of the trial court in the High Court. In Gobind Prasad vs Hari Dutt, AIR 1977 SC 1005, the above views were reaffirmed by Kailasam, J observing "It is settled law that fixation of the period within which the contract has to be performed does not make the stipulation as to time the essence of the contract. When a contract relates to sale of immovable property it will normally be presumed that the time is not the essence of the contract. The intention to treat time as the essence of the contract may be evidenced by the circumstances which are sufficiently strong to displace the normal presumption that is a contract of sale of land stipulation as to time is not of the essence of the contract". 

 25. In the later case, an agreement was executed between Kamal Rani and Chand Rani on 26th August, 1971 in which Kamal Rani agreed to sell her house at Rs 178,000 and received Rs 30,000 as advance from Chand Rani Stipulating that Rs 98,000 payable within 10 days and the balance at the time of registration of deed. It was also agreed that the vendor would redeem the property by paying loan of Rs. 25,000 and she was also to obtain income tax clearance. The sale deed to be executed before 31st October, 1911. Chand Rani called upon to complete the sale by various letters but she did not get response. On the other hand, Kamal Rani claimed that since Chand Rani failed to pay Rs. 98,000 within 10 days as agreed, the agreement stood cancelled and issued a letter on 15th August, 1971. The trial Court decreed the suit and the High Court held that the transaction failed on account of non-payment of Rs 98,000 and set-aside the decree for specific performance. The Supreme Court affirmed the judgment of the High Court on the reasoning that 'the plaintiff was never willing to make the payment of Rs 98000 even on 27th September, 1971'. Though the Supreme Court affirmed the High Court's judgment, approved its previous opinions on the question of the consequence of non performance of contract for sale of immovable property within the specified time observing in paragraph 24 that "in case of sale of immovable property there is no presumption as to time being the essence of the contract. Even it is not of the essence of the contract the court may infer that it is to be performed in a. reasonable time if the conditions are 1from the express terms of the contract; 2. from the nature of the property; and 3. from the surrounding circumstances, for example; the object of making the contract". In that case the defendant issued notices reminding the plaintiff to pay Rs 98,000 for redemption of the mortgage against which the plaintiff was asking for handing over possession of the first floor by 30th September, 1971. Under such circumstances, the Supreme Court came to the conclusion that "even as late as 24-9-1991 the plaintiff was never willing to make the payment of Rs 98,000. In this connection we have already seen the oral evidence. It shows there was no readiness and willingness". This case is quite distinguishable and not applicable in the instant case.
